claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a nominal fcc matrix.
High-temperature degradation is governed by the stability and integrity of a protective Al-/Cr-rich oxide scale.
High oxygen partial pressure causes rapid oxide-scale thickening.
Rapid oxide-scale growth generates excessive growth stresses.
Excessive oxide growth stresses cause scale cracking and spallation.
Hydrogen addition under reducing conditions promotes oxygen-vacancy formation in the protective oxide.
Hydrogen chemically reduces and destabilizes the protective oxide scale.
Chemical destabilization of the scale undermines its barrier properties.
Breakdown of the oxide barrier promotes internal oxidation and non-uniform scale degradation.
Oxidative and hydrogen-assisted scale-instability mechanisms create localized stress concentrations at the oxide–metal interface.
Localized interfacial stress concentrations eventually trigger catastrophic failure.
At oxygen partial pressures above the air baseline, oxide scales will be thicker and more brittle than in standard air.
At oxygen partial pressures above the air baseline, spallation and crack propagation will begin earlier than in standard air.
Increasing hydrogen concentration from 5% to 20% will produce progressively greater chemical degradation and non-uniformity of the oxide scale.
Hydrogen-containing exposures will accelerate internal oxidation relative to standard-air exposure without added hydrogen.
Hydrogen-containing exposures will cause earlier mechanical failure than the standard-air baseline.
The proposed controlled test varies oxygen partial pressure among 0.1, 0.21, and 1 atm and separately varies hydrogen concentration among 5%, 10%, and 20% at 900°C.
The proposed behavior is expected to apply near 900°C after exposure times sufficient to produce measurable scale features.
